study_identification.author_journal_year: Jing et al., Human Brain Mapping, 2023
study_identification.title: Heterogeneous brain dynamic functional connectivity patterns in first-episode drug-naive patients with major depressive disorder

study_characteristics.study_objective: To identify subtypes of first-episode drug-naive (FEDN) major depressive disorder (MDD) patients based on dynamic functional connectivity patterns using normative modeling and unsupervised machine learning, and to characterize their biological and clinical heterogeneity.

dataset_name.answer: International Big-Data Center for Depression Research (IBCDR)

hc_n.answer: 91 (healthy-base group matched to patients); 125 (healthy-ICA group for independent component analysis)

hc_age.answer: Healthy-base group: mean 32.49; SD 11.79; Healthy-ICA group: mean 31.11; SD 8.50

hc_sex.answer: Healthy-base group: F 26 (28.6%), M 65 (71.4%); Healthy-ICA group: F 54 (43.2%), M 71 (56.8%)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: DPARSF software (http://www.rfmri.org/DPARSF); AAL template (90 ROIs); GIG-ICA (group information guided independent component analysis) for dynamic functional connectivity extraction; Sliding time window method (window length = 60s, step size = 1)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Subjects with excessive head motion excluded (mean FD <= 0.5 mm or max FD <= 2 mm). Mean FD: Healthy-base 0.07±0.03 mm, Healthy-ICA 0.06±0.04 mm, FEDN-MDD 0.07±0.04 mm; Max FD: Healthy-base 0.44±0.38 mm, Healthy-ICA 0.37±0.37 mm, FEDN-MDD 0.40±0.37 mm.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: To avoid center effect, only subjects from the same center were included in the analysis (164 healthy controls and 91 FEDN-MDD patients from one center). An independent sample of 125 healthy controls from two other centers with similar data acquisition was used as the healthy-ICA group to create group-level components.

modeling_method.answer: Second-order polynomial regression normative model with quantile regression approach

software_tool.answer: Custom implementation (details in supplementary materials); R matchIt function for group matching; GIG-ICA for feature extraction; k-means clustering

response_variable.answer: 20 IC measures (global efficiency coefficient of each independent component); 20 fluctuation coefficients (average change of frame-wise variation of each IC's time-varying weights)

predictor_effects.answer: Age was modeled as a predictor in the normative model. The model estimated 5th, 50th (median), and 95th percentiles of each feature as a function of age.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addressed some nuisance factors (age, sex, education as covariates in group comparisons; motion parameters as exclusion criteria) but the normative model itself only included age as a predictor. Site effects were handled by restricting analysis to a single center rather than modeling site as a nuisance variable. Sex and other potential confounds were not explicitly modeled in the normative model construction, though they were used as covariates in subsequent statistical tests.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: After obtaining the 20 IC measures and 20 fluctuation coefficients of each healthy-base control, we built the second-order polynomial regression normative model... on the relationship between age and these 40 features, respectively. ... Pseudo two sample t-tests were conducted to explore the functional connectivity differences of the ICs between healthy-based controls and subtypes of FEDN-MDD using statistical nonparametric mapping software (SnPM13... permutation tests n = 5000, age, sex and education as covariates). ... To avoid the center effect, 164 healthy individuals and 91 FEDN-MDD patients... from the same center were included.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study used 10-fold cross-validation to build and assess the normative model, which involves using subsets of the same training dataset (healthy-base controls) for validation. This is a form of same-domain non-independent validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To assess generalization, we applied 10-fold cross-validation to build an aggregation normative model for each feature (details in supplementary materials). The average value of the 10 individual z scores yielded from the normative aggregation model was the final feature deviation for each individual.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study did not use an independent holdout set of healthy controls from the same dataset/domain to validate the normative model. The only validation mentioned is 10-fold cross-validation within the training data.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: To assess generalization, we applied 10-fold cross-validation to build an aggregation normative model for each feature

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study did not validate the normative model using healthy controls from a different dataset or acquisition site. The healthy-ICA group from two other centers was used only for generating group-level ICA components, not for validating the normative model.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Another independent sample (125 control individuals, 71 females) from the other two centers with similar data acquisition was a healthy-ICA group to create the group-level components as guidance information in ICA.

clinical_dataset.answer: International Big-Data Center for Depression Research (IBCDR) - same center as healthy controls

clinical_groups_n.answer: FEDN-MDD:91 (89 included in final clustering after excluding 2 with low clustering certainty)

clinical_groups_age.answer: FEDN-MDD overall: 34.80±9.49 years; Subtype I: 35.36±8.12 years; Subtype II: 34.73±9.77 years

deviation_metric.answer: Normalized z-score quantifying deviation from normative range. For each individual i and feature f of IC j, deviation calculated as: z_ijf = (C_real - C_50th) / (C_95th - C_5th), where C_real is the observed value, C_50th is the predicted median, and C_5th and C_95th are the 5th and 95th percentiles. Each patient characterized by 40-dimensional feature vector (20 IC measures' deviations + 20 fluctuation coefficients' deviations).

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Multivariate unsupervised k-means clustering with forward feature selection (100 repeated runs) to identify subtypes based on deviation patterns. Clustering reliability assessed using certainty measure (subjects with certainty <0.6 excluded, n=2). Group differences in functional connectivity tested using pseudo two-sample t-tests with permutation testing (SnPM13, n=5000 permutations, age/sex/education as covariates). VBM analysis with pseudo two-sample t-tests (n=10000 permutations, age/sex/education/TIV as covariates) to compare gray matter between subtypes and healthy controls. Clinical variables (HAMD, HAMA, illness duration) compared between subtypes.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Two FEDN-MDD subtypes were identified: Subtype I (16%, n=14) with larger extreme deviations from normal range and shorter illness duration (11.75±12.09 months); Subtype II (84%, n=75) with weaker deviations and longer illness duration (22.1±23.92 months, p=.03).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Two subtypes of FEDN-MDD were identified using normative modeling and unsupervised clustering. Twelve informative features from 10 independent components (ICs) were selected, involving DMN, frontoparietal networks, ACC-hub, visual, language-related, bilateral executive control, hippocampus-hub, thalamus-hub, and caudate-hub networks. Subtype I (n=14, 16%) showed larger extreme deviations in functional characteristics and shorter illness duration (11.75±12.09 months), with more widespread functional connectivity abnormalities across all informative networks. Compared to healthy controls, Subtype I showed both increased and decreased functional connectivity between frontal and occipital cortex in DMN, and mostly decreased gray matter in temporal cortex and anterior cingulate gyrus. Subtype II (n=75, 84%) had weaker deviations, longer illness duration (22.1±23.92 months, p=.03), and mostly decreased functional connectivity in DMN. Subtype II showed more complex structural changes with both increased gray matter (mainly middle frontal and posterior regions) and decreased gray matter (mainly temporal and superior frontal regions) widely distributed. Depression severity (HAMD) and anxiety severity (HAMA) did not differ between subtypes (p>.05). Mean silhouette index was 0.461, instability of cluster centers was 4.08, and mean clustering stability was 0.97.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: 1) Study included only treatment-naive patients, so findings may not generalize to MDD groups with multiple prior episodes or active antidepressant therapy. 2) K-means clustering has limitations as it seeks only compact clusters; more powerful clustering methods capable of detecting diverse cluster types would be ideal. 3) The number of ICs (20) was empirically determined rather than automatically estimated. 4) Cross-sectional design lacks treatment information, so value of this clustering for treatment prediction remains unknown. 5) Limited generalizability due to small sample size of Subtype I (n=14) in this specific FEDN cohort. 6) Illness duration range is relatively limited (Subtype I: ~11 months, Subtype II: ~22 months), limiting conclusions about relationship between illness duration and brain changes. 7) Data from a single center to avoid site effects may limit external validity.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates that FEDN-MDD is heterogeneous and can be parsed into biologically distinct subtypes based on individualized deviation patterns from normative functional connectivity. The combination of normative modeling with unsupervised clustering provides a data-driven approach to subtyping that goes beyond conventional case-control comparisons. The findings suggest that altered brain function becomes more convergent as illness duration increases, though this needs confirmation in larger samples with wider illness duration ranges. The approach could potentially be extended to predict treatment response in future longitudinal studies.

general_notes.general_notes: This study applies normative modeling to dynamic functional connectivity patterns (not static structural measures) in FEDN-MDD. The normative model was built using quantile regression to estimate 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles as a function of age, allowing characterization of individual deviations from the normal range. The study used GIG-ICA to extract 20 independent components and computed both connectivity strength (IC measures) and temporal variability (fluctuation coefficients) for each component. Forward feature selection identified 12 informative features from 10 ICs for clustering. The study is notable for its focus on first-episode drug-naive patients, avoiding confounds from medication effects or chronicity. However, the normative model only included age as a predictor, not accounting for sex, site, or other potential confounds within the model itself (these were handled through matching or covariate adjustment in subsequent analyses). The clustering approach involved 100 repeated runs to ensure stability, with only 2 patients excluded due to low clustering certainty. The study found that functional and structural brain changes differ between subtypes, with Subtype I showing more extreme deviations but less complex patterns compared to Subtype II. This suggests heterogeneity in the pathophysiology and progression of MDD even in first-episode patients. Dataset acquisition parameters are mentioned to be in supplementary materials (Table S1) but were not accessible in the markdown conversion.
